meaning: どう頑張ってもそこまでが限度、という精一杯のところ。
origin: 「関」は東海道の宿場町・関宿（三重県亀山市）、「山」は祭りの山車。関神社の祭りの山車があまりに豪華で「これ以上の贅沢はできない」と言われたから、あるいは狭い宿場の道幅いっぱいに山車が練り歩いたから、という二つの説がある。
example: この予算では現状維持が関の山だ。

sources.label: 地域文化資産ポータル（関の山車）

en.meaning: The utmost one can do; the limit that no amount of effort will get past.
en.origin: Seki refers to Seki-juku, a post town on the Tōkaidō in what is now Kameyama, Mie Prefecture, and yama to festival floats (dashi). There are two theories: that the floats of the Seki Shrine festival were so lavish people said no greater extravagance was possible, or that the floats filled the full width of the post town's narrow street as they paraded through.
en.example: With this budget, keeping things as they are is the best we can manage.

meaning: 武芸や相撲で、天下に並ぶ者がいないほど強いこと。また、その人。ふつうは横綱の異称。
origin: 「日下」は天下、「開山」は寺の開祖。1682年に「天下一」を名乗ることが禁じられ、武芸者や芸能者が代わりに使い始めた。江戸後期には横綱免許を受けた大関を指し、明治ごろから横綱の別称になった。「ひのしたかいざん」とも読む。
example: 全勝で賜杯を抱いた新横綱は、日下開山の名にふさわしかった。

en.meaning: So strong in martial arts or sumo that no one in the land is a match; also, such a person. Usually used as another name for a yokozuna.
en.origin: Hinoshita (日下) means the whole realm, and kaisan (開山) is the founder of a temple. In 1682 calling oneself tenka-ichi (best in the realm) was banned, and martial artists and performers began using this term instead. In the late Edo period it referred to an ōzeki who had received a yokozuna license, and from around the Meiji era it became another name for yokozuna. It is also read hinoshita kaizan.
en.example: The new yokozuna, who took the Emperor's Cup with a perfect record, lived up to the title of hinoshita kaisan.

meaning: 惚れた相手なら、欠点さえ長所に見えてしまう。ひいき目で見ればどんな欠点も良く見える、というたとえ。
origin: 「痘痕」は天然痘が治ったあとに残る肌のくぼみ、「靨」は笑うと頬にできるくぼみ。初出は洒落本『伊賀越増補合羽之龍』（1779年）。「良く見えているだけ」という皮肉を含むので、本人たちに向けて言うと角が立つ。
example: 惚れた相手の遅刻癖まで愛嬌に見えるのだから、痘痕も靨だ。

en.meaning: When you are in love with someone, even their faults look like good points. A figure for how partiality makes any flaw look attractive.
en.origin: Abata (痘痕) are the pits left in the skin after recovering from smallpox, and ekubo (靨) are the dimples that form in the cheeks when smiling. The earliest known use is in the sharebon Igagoe Zōho Kappa no Tatsu (1779). Because the phrase carries the irony that the faults only look good, saying it to the couple themselves can give offense.
en.example: When even the habit of showing up late looks charming in the one you love, love really is blind.

meaning: 見かけはいいが中身が伴わないもの。人について言うときは「食わせ者」と書き、さりげなく見せて実は油断ならない人物を指す。
origin: 「食わす」には古く、相手に不利益をかぶせる・欺くという意味があった。そこから「人を欺くもの」の意味になった。
example: とんだ食わせ物をつかまされた。／あの男は相当の食わせ者だ。

en.meaning: Something that looks good but has nothing behind it. Said of a person, it is written 食わせ者 and refers to someone who seems unassuming but is in fact not to be trusted.
en.origin: The verb kuwasu once also meant to saddle someone with a loss, or to deceive them. From this the word came to mean something that deceives people.
en.example: I got stuck with a real dud. / That man is a crafty one.

meaning: ハレ（晴）は祭りや年中行事、冠婚葬祭などの非日常。ケ（褻）は普段の日常生活。
origin: 柳田國男が民俗学の概念として広めたが、言葉自体は古く、1603年の『日葡辞書』にも載っている。「晴れ着」「晴れ舞台」のハレはこれ。1970年代以降は、ケのエネルギーが枯れた状態としての「ケガレ」を加えて論じられることもある。
example: 祭りや正月はハレ、それ以外の普段の暮らしはケにあたる。

sources.label: ハレとケの意味と由来

en.meaning: Hare (晴) is the out-of-the-ordinary: festivals, annual observances, and ceremonial occasions such as weddings and funerals. Ke (褻) is ordinary everyday life.
en.origin: Yanagita Kunio popularized the pair as a concept in folklore studies, but the words themselves are old and appear in the 1603 Nippo Jisho. The hare in haregi (one's best clothes) and harebutai (a grand occasion, a time in the spotlight) is this hare. Since the 1970s the pair has sometimes been discussed together with kegare, understood as the state in which the energy of ke has run dry.
en.example: Festivals and New Year are hare, and the rest of ordinary life is ke.

meaning: 威勢がよく、さっぱりしていて粋なさま。また、そういう気風の若者。
origin: 語源は諸説あり、日本国語大辞典は未詳とする。魚河岸の若者が結った、イナ(ボラの若魚)の背に似た髷「鯔背銀杏」から来たとする説もある。文政(1818〜30)ごろの佃節では神田の若者の気風が「いなせ」と歌われた。守貞漫稿によれば人柄や品物にも使い、ほめ言葉とは限らなかった。
example: 法被を着た課長は、いつもと違っていなせに見えた。

en.meaning: Spirited, straightforward, and stylish; also, a young person with that kind of temperament.
en.origin: There are several theories about its origin, and the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten lists it as unknown. One theory traces it to inase-ichō, a topknot worn by the young men of the fish market that resembled the back of an ina (a young gray mullet). In Tsukuda-bushi songs from around the Bunsei era (1818 to 1830), the spirit of the young men of Kanda was sung of as inase. According to the Morisada Mankō, the word was also applied to people's character and to goods, and was not always a compliment.
en.example: Wearing a happi coat, the section chief looked unusually dashing.

meaning: 頼みや相談を、取りつく島もないほど無愛想にはねつけるさま。
origin: 「けん」も「ほろろ」も雉の鳴き声とされ、「ほろろ」は羽音とする説もある。「けん」に「けんどん(慳貪)」「けんつく(剣突)」のとげとげしさを掛けたものという。古い例は天草本伊曾保物語(1593)に見える。
example: 企画を持ち込んだが、部長にけんもほろろに断られた。

en.meaning: Turning down a request or proposal so bluntly that there is nothing left to hold on to.
en.origin: Both ken and hororo are said to be the cry of the pheasant, and one theory holds that hororo is the sound of its wings. The ken is said to play on the harshness of kendon (慳貪, stingy and cold) and kentsuku (剣突, a sharp rebuke). An early example appears in the Amakusa edition of Isoho Monogatari (Aesop's Fables) of 1593.
en.example: I brought the proposal to the department head and was flatly turned down.

meaning: 相手のためを装いながら、実は自分の得を図ること。
origin: 「ごかし」は動詞「こかす(転かす)」の連用形「こかし」が濁ったもので、何かを口実にして自分の利を図る意を添える接尾語。「親切ごかし」も同じ形。浄瑠璃『祇園女御九重錦』(1760)に用例がある。
example: 「君のためを思って」という忠告は、ただのおためごかしだった。

en.meaning: Pretending to act for someone else's sake while actually serving one's own interest.
en.origin: Gokashi is the voiced form of kokashi, the continuative form of the verb kokasu (転かす, to tip over). As a suffix it adds the sense of using something as a pretext to serve oneself. Shinsetsu-gokashi (feigned kindness) has the same form. An example appears in the jōruri play Gion Nyōgo Kokonoe no Nishiki (1760).
en.example: The advice offered "for your own good" was nothing but self-interest dressed up as concern.

meaning: ある物事の範囲の外。関心や検討の対象から外れていること。
origin: 「埒」はもともと馬場の周りに巡らした柵。そこから物事の区切り・範囲の意味が生まれ、中世後期ごろには「埒が明く」のような使い方が始まっていたとみられる。字通は「埒が明く」を上賀茂神社の競馬(くらべうま)神事から出た語とする。
example: 出世は彼の関心の埒外にある。

en.meaning: Outside the scope of a matter; outside what one cares about or is considering.
en.origin: Rachi (埒) was originally the fence built around a riding ground. From this came the sense of a division or scope, and by around the late medieval period usages such as rachi ga aku (a matter gets settled) appear to have begun. The Jitsū dictionary says rachi ga aku came from the kurabeuma horse-race ritual at Kamigamo Shrine.
en.example: Getting promoted lies outside the bounds of his interests.

meaning: 正体がはっきりせず怪しいこと。また、真偽が疑わしいこと。
origin: 「う」「ろん」はともに「胡」「乱」の唐音。正法眼蔵や五山僧の詩文に見えることから、禅宗を通じて伝わった語とみられる。中国では「乱雑」の意味だったが、日本で「疑わしい」の意味が派生し、のちにこちらが主になった。
example: 駅前で胡乱な儲け話を持ちかけられた。

en.meaning: Of uncertain identity and suspicious; also, of doubtful truth.
en.origin: U and ron are the tōon readings of 胡 and 乱. Because the word appears in the Shōbōgenzō and in the poetry and prose of Gozan monks, it is thought to have come in through Zen Buddhism. In China it meant disorderly, but in Japan the sense of doubtful developed and later became the main one.
en.example: Outside the station, someone pitched me a shady moneymaking scheme.

meaning: いろいろあった末の結局のところ。たいていは思わしくない結果について言う。
origin: 出世魚のボラは成長につれて名前が変わり、最後に「トド」と呼ばれる。そこから「行き着く果て」の意味になった。洒落本『京伝予誌』(1790)に用例がある。
example: 何度も会議を重ねたが、とどのつまり現状維持に落ち着いた。

en.gloss: in the end, when all is said and done
en.meaning: Ultimately, after everything that has happened. Usually said of an unwelcome outcome.
en.origin: The gray mullet (bora) is a shusse-uo, a fish whose name changes as it grows, and at its final stage it is called todo. From this the phrase came to mean where things end up. An example appears in the sharebon Kyōden Yoshi (1790).
en.example: We held meeting after meeting, but in the end we settled on keeping things as they were.

meaning: 自分は見聞が狭いので、と謙遜して「知らない」と言うときの前置き。
origin: 「寡聞」は見聞が狭いこと。字通は出典として『礼記』学記篇の、独りで学んで友がいなければ見聞が狭くなる、という一節を挙げる。日本では空海の『三教指帰』(797ごろ)に早い例がある。
example: 寡聞にして、そのような規則があるとは存じませんでした。

en.meaning: A humble preface used when saying one does not know something, putting it down to one's own narrow learning.
en.origin: Kabun (寡聞) means having heard and seen little. The Jitsū dictionary gives as its source a passage in the Xueji chapter of the Book of Rites (Liji) saying that one who studies alone without friends will have narrow knowledge. In Japan an early example is in Kūkai's Sangō Shiiki (around 797).
en.example: In my limited knowledge, I was not aware that any such rule existed.

meaning: 酒や芸事のたしなみがないことを、へりくだって言う言葉。手際が悪いことや、しくじり・不始末の意味もある。
origin: 「手際が悪い」の意味では高野山文書(1283)に例があるほど古い。「しくじり」の意味は狂言『栗焼』に、酒や芸事に疎いと謙遜する意味は狂言『庖丁聟』に見える。
example: 酒のほうはとんと不調法でして。

en.gloss: having no head for drink or the arts
en.meaning: A humble way of saying one has no taste or skill for drinking or the performing arts. It can also mean clumsiness, or a blunder or misconduct.
en.origin: The sense of clumsiness is old enough to appear in the Kōyasan documents of 1283. The sense of a blunder is found in the kyōgen play Kuriyaki, and the humble sense of being a stranger to drink or the arts in the kyōgen play Hōchō Muko.
en.example: I'm afraid I'm not much of a drinker.

meaning: ゆったりと構えて、小さなことにこだわらないさま。
origin: もとは『詩経』大雅に出る漢語で、鷹が飛び立つような武威ある姿を言った。日本では意味と音の近い和語「大様(おおよう)」と混同され、近世以降はほぼ「大様」の意味で使われている。
example: 社長は少しの遅刻には目くじらを立てない鷹揚な人だ。

en.meaning: Relaxed and generous, not fussing over small things.
en.origin: It was originally a Chinese word from the Daya section of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), describing a martial bearing like a hawk taking flight. In Japan it was confused with the native word ōyō (大様, read おおよう), which is close in meaning and sound, and since the early modern period it has been used almost entirely in the sense of 大様.
en.example: The president is easygoing and doesn't make a fuss when someone is a little late.

meaning: 身の程知らずの言動がばかばかしく、見ていて苦々しいさま。
origin: 古語「傍(かたはら)痛し」(そばで見ていていたたまれない)が元。この「かたはら」が「片腹」と解されて今の表記になった。平安中期の『小右記』(1014)にすでに「片腹痛」の字が見える。脇腹が痛いという意味ではない。
example: 入社したばかりの新人に段取りを説かれるとは片腹痛い。

en.meaning: Ridiculous and galling to watch, said of words or actions by someone who does not know their place.
en.origin: It comes from the classical katahara itashi (傍痛し, painful to watch from the side, hard to bear witnessing). This katahara was later taken to mean 片腹 (one side of the belly), giving the current spelling. The characters 片腹痛 already appear in the mid-Heian diary Shōyūki (1014). It does not mean having a pain in one's side.
en.example: Being lectured on how to organize the work by a newcomer who just joined the company is laughable.

meaning: その人の力量に比べて、与えられた役目が軽すぎること。
origin: もとは割り当てられた役に不満を持つことを言った。「自分には荷が重い」の意味で使うのは本来の用法ではない。文化庁の世論調査で「力量に対して役目が重すぎる」を選んだ人は平成14年度62.8%から令和6年度48.9%に減り、本来の「軽すぎる」は27.6%から45.1%に増えた。
example: 彼女に議事録係では役不足だ。

en.meaning: Of an assigned role, too minor for the person's ability.
en.origin: It originally meant being dissatisfied with the role one had been given. Using it to mean the role is too much for oneself is not the original usage. In the Agency for Cultural Affairs public opinion survey on the Japanese language, the share choosing "a role too heavy for one's ability" fell from 62.8% in fiscal Heisei 14 (2002) to 48.9% in fiscal Reiwa 6 (2024), while the original "too light" rose from 27.6% to 45.1%.
en.example: Taking minutes is a role too small for her.

meaning: 気遣いや遠慮をする必要がなく、心から打ち解けられるさま。
origin: 「気を置く」(気兼ねする)の打ち消しなので、ほめ言葉になる。文化庁の世論調査では、本来の「遠慮しなくてよい」が平成14年度44.6%、平成24年度42.7%。逆の「遠慮しなくてはならない」は40.1%から47.6%に増え、平成18年度以降はこちらが上回っている。
example: 学生時代からの気が置けない友人とは、何でも話せる。

en.meaning: Needing no reserve or carefulness; someone you can be completely at ease with.
en.origin: It is the negative of ki o oku (to feel constrained), so it is a compliment. In the Agency for Cultural Affairs public opinion survey, the original meaning, "no need to hold back," was chosen by 44.6% in fiscal Heisei 14 (2002) and 42.7% in fiscal Heisei 24 (2012). The opposite, "one has to hold back," rose from 40.1% to 47.6%, and has come out ahead since fiscal Heisei 18 (2006).
en.example: I can talk about anything with my friends from school, whom I never have to be on guard around.

meaning: その場しのぎで間に合わせること。根本的な解決を先送りするやり方。
origin: 「姑」はしばらく、「息」は休むの意。『礼記』檀弓上で、曾子が君子の徳による愛し方と対比して、細人(小人)の愛し方を「姑息」と言ったのが出典。「ひきょうな」の意味で使うのは近年の用法で、文化庁の世論調査では「姑息な手段」を「ひきょうな」と取る人が平成22年度70.9%、令和3年度73.9%。本来の「一時しのぎ」は15.0%から17.4%にとどまる。
example: 再起動で済ませるのは姑息な手段で、根本の修正にはならない。

en.meaning: Making do for the moment; an approach that puts off a real solution.
en.origin: Ko (姑) means for a while and soku (息) means to rest. The source is the Tangong I chapter of the Book of Rites, where Zengzi contrasts the way a gentleman loves through virtue with the way a petty person loves, calling the latter kosoku. Using it to mean underhanded is a recent usage. In the Agency for Cultural Affairs public opinion survey, 70.9% in fiscal Heisei 22 (2010) and 73.9% in fiscal Reiwa 3 (2021) took kosoku na shudan to mean "an underhanded method," while the original "a temporary fix" stayed at 15.0% and 17.4%.
en.example: Restarting it is only a stopgap and doesn't fix the underlying problem.

meaning: おもしろくない。あまり感心しない。
origin: 「ぞっと」には恐怖や寒さのほか、強く心を動かされて身震いする意味もある。「ぞっとしない」はその打ち消しで「心が動かない」を表す。文化庁の世論調査で「余りぞっとしない映画」を「面白くない」と取った人は平成18年度31.3%、平成28年度22.8%。「恐ろしくない」は54.1%から56.1%だった。
example: そのリメイクは映像こそきれいだが、筋はぞっとしない。

en.gloss: not much to get excited about
en.meaning: Not interesting; not very impressive.
en.origin: Besides fear or cold, zotto can also mean shuddering from being strongly moved. Zotto shinai is its negative and means not being moved. In the Agency for Cultural Affairs public opinion survey, the share who took amari zotto shinai eiga to mean "a film that is not very interesting" was 31.3% in fiscal Heisei 18 (2006) and 22.8% in fiscal Heisei 28 (2016). The share who took it as "not frightening" went from 54.1% to 56.1%.
en.example: The remake looks beautiful, but the plot is nothing to get excited about.

meaning: 喜んでそうする。進んで協力する気がある。
origin: 古くは物惜しみする意の「やふさし」「やふさがる」があり、その語幹「やふさ」に接尾語「か」が付いて「やぶさか」ができた。本来は「けち・思い切りが悪い」の意で、その打ち消しなので「惜しまずやる」になる。文化庁の平成25年度調査では、本来の「喜んでする」が33.8%、「仕方なくする」が43.7%だった。
example: 条件次第では、幹事を引き受けるのも吝かでない。

en.meaning: Glad to do something; ready to help.
en.origin: Older Japanese had yafusashi and yafusagaru, meaning to be grudging, and adding the suffix ka to their stem yafusa produced yabusaka. The original sense was stingy or hesitant, so its negative means doing something without holding back. In the Agency for Cultural Affairs survey for fiscal Heisei 25 (2013), 33.8% chose the original "do it gladly" and 43.7% chose "do it reluctantly."
en.example: Depending on the terms, I'd be willing to take on organizing the party.

meaning: 少しも眠らずに。一睡もしないで夜を明かすさま。
origin: 「まんじり」はちょっと眠る様子を表す副詞で、打ち消しを伴って「一睡もしない」を強める。文化庁の平成25年度調査では、本来の意味とされる「眠らないで」が28.7%、「じっと動かないで」が51.5%で逆転していた。
example: 合否の連絡が気になって、まんじりともせず夜を明かした。

en.meaning: Without sleeping at all; staying awake through the night.
en.origin: Manjiri is an adverb describing a brief doze, and with a negative it emphasizes not sleeping a wink. In the Agency for Cultural Affairs survey for fiscal Heisei 25 (2013), the meaning considered original, "without sleeping," was chosen by 28.7%, and "without moving" by 51.5%, so the two had reversed.
en.example: Anxious to hear whether I had passed, I spent the night without sleeping a wink.

meaning: 世間の経験を積み、物事の裏も表も知り尽くしたずる賢さ。また、そういうしたたかな人。
origin: 海に千年、山に千年すんだ蛇は竜になるという言い伝えから。江戸から明治にかけては「海に千年山に千年」という長い形が普通だった。四字に縮めた「海千山千」の用例は大正期から見られ、比較的新しい言い方である。
example: 相手は海千山千の交渉役だから、こちらの手の内は読まれていると思ったほうがいい。

en.meaning: The cunning of someone who has seen a great deal of the world and knows all its ins and outs; also, such a hardened person.
en.origin: From the belief that a snake that has lived a thousand years in the sea and a thousand years in the mountains becomes a dragon. From the Edo period into the Meiji era the longer form umi ni sennen yama ni sennen was usual. Examples of the shortened four-character form umisen yamasen appear from the Taishō era, making it a relatively new expression.
en.example: The other side's negotiator is a wily old hand, so assume they can already read our cards.

meaning: 当事者より、はたで見ている者のほうが物事の真相や得失をよく見抜けるということ。「傍目八目」とも書く。
origin: 囲碁から出た言葉で、江戸初期の俳諧の参考書『世話尽』に囲碁の用語として載る。「岡」は直接かかわりのない立場を表し、「岡目」は傍観者のこと。「八目」は八手先まで読めるという解釈が広く行われているが、「目」は地を数える単位なので八目分得をする手が見えるという意味だとする説もある。
example: 岡目八目というから、自分の企画書は人に読んでもらうことにしている。

en.gloss: onlookers see more of the game
en.meaning: People watching from the side can see the truth of a matter, and what is to be gained or lost, better than those involved. Also written 傍目八目.
en.origin: The phrase comes from go and is listed as a go term in Sewa Zukushi, an early Edo-period reference book for haikai. Oka indicates a position with no direct involvement, and okame means an onlooker. Hachimoku is widely interpreted as being able to read eight moves ahead, but another theory holds that since moku is a unit for counting territory, it means seeing moves that gain eight points.
en.example: Onlookers see more of the game, so I make a point of having someone else read my proposals.

meaning: 数ばかり多くて取るに足りない人や物。集まったつまらない連中を見下して言う。
origin: 仏教語の「有相無相」から出た言葉で、もとは形のあるものもないものも含めたすべての存在を指した。そこから雑多なものの意に広がり、さらにくだらない連中を卑しめる言い方になった。後者の意味では1763年の『川柳評万句合』に用例がある。
example: 炎上すると有象無象が集まってきて、本題が見えなくなる。

en.meaning: People or things that are many in number but of no account. Used contemptuously of a crowd of worthless people.
en.origin: It comes from the Buddhist term 有相無相, which originally referred to all that exists, things with form and things without. From there it broadened to mean a miscellaneous jumble, and then became a disparaging term for worthless people. In the latter sense an example appears in the Senryū-hyō Mankuawase of 1763.
en.example: Once something blows up online, all sorts of riffraff pile on and the real issue gets lost.

meaning: 人をだましたり、思いどおりに操ったりするための手口やかけひき。
origin: 「手練（てれん）」も「手管（てくだ）」も人をだます手段のことで、同じ意味の語を重ねて強めた表現。どちらも語源のはっきりしない和語で、漢字は当て字である。1715年の談義本『艶道通鑑』に用例が見える。
example: 手練手管を尽くして社長に取り入り、役員の座についた。

en.meaning: The ploys and maneuvering used to deceive people or manipulate them at will.
en.origin: Both teren (手練) and tekuda (手管) mean a way of deceiving people, and the phrase pairs two words of the same meaning for emphasis. Both are native words of unclear origin, and the kanji are ateji (characters used for their sound). An example appears in the dangibon Endō Tsugan of 1715.
en.example: Using every wile and trick, they wormed their way into the president's favor and landed a seat on the board.

meaning: 数が多くても値段がひどく安いこと。投げ売り同然の値段。
origin: 丈夫な金剛草履が二足でわずか三文だったことから出たとされる。そのため古くは「二足三文」とも書いた。江戸初期の咄本『きのふはけふの物語』に用例がある。
example: 実家の古い家具は二束三文にしかならなかった。

en.meaning: Extremely cheap even in quantity; a price as low as a clearance sale.
en.origin: It is said to come from sturdy kongō zōri sandals selling for a mere three mon for two pairs. For this reason it was also written 二足三文 in the past. An example appears in the early Edo-period hanashibon Kinō wa Kyō no Monogatari.
en.example: The old furniture from my parents' house sold for next to nothing.

meaning: 持っている服の中でいちばん上等な、とっておきの一着。もとは替えのない一枚きりの服も指した。
origin: 予備のない一本きりのろうそくを指した「一挺蝋（いっちょうろう）」がなまった語とする説がある。それが「一枚きりの羅（うすぎぬ）」の意で「一張羅」と書かれるようになったという。用例は1687年の浮世草子『男色大鑑』に見える。
example: 一張羅のスーツを着て結婚式に出た。

en.meaning: The finest piece of clothing one owns, kept for special occasions. Originally it also meant the only garment one had, with nothing to change into.
en.origin: One theory holds that it is a corruption of icchōrō (一挺蝋), a single candle with no spare. This is said to have come to be written 一張羅 in the sense of a single garment of ra (thin silk). An example appears in the ukiyo-zōshi Nanshoku Ōkagami of 1687.
en.example: I wore my one good suit to the wedding.

meaning: 無口で愛想のない人。また、気がきかず物の道理が分からない人をののしって言う。
origin: 日本で作られた和製漢語とみられ、語源ははっきりしない。漢字は当て字で、「朴」は素朴・朴訥の飾り気のなさ、「念」は思い、「仁」は人を表すと説明される。江戸後期の滑稽本『浮世風呂』に用例がある。
example: 何を話しかけても「ああ」としか返さない朴念仁で、会話が続かない。

en.meaning: A taciturn, unfriendly person. Also used as an insult for someone tactless who does not understand how things work.
en.origin: It appears to be a Chinese-style compound coined in Japan (wasei kango), and its origin is unclear. The kanji are ateji: boku (朴) is explained as the plainness of soboku and bokutotsu, nen (念) as thought, and jin (仁) as person. An example appears in the late Edo-period comic book (kokkeibon) Ukiyoburo.
en.example: Whatever you say to them, all you get back is "Yeah." They are such a bokunenjin that the conversation goes nowhere.

meaning: 気がきかない人や、話の通じないわからず屋をののしる言葉。
origin: 語源ははっきりしない。センダンやチャンチンの別名として唐変木と呼ぶ例があり、もとは「唐から来た変わった木」を指した可能性がある。そこへ道理の分からない人をののしる「唐人」が重なり、人への悪口になったとする見方がある。1783年の洒落本『卯地臭意』に「とうへんぼくめ」の用例がある。
example: 何度説明しても同じことを聞き返してくる唐変木だ。

en.meaning: An insult for someone tactless, or someone unreasonable who will not listen.
en.origin: The origin is unclear. Tōhenboku is recorded as another name for the chinaberry (sendan) and the Chinese mahogany (chanchin), so it may originally have meant an odd tree from China. One view holds that this overlapped with tōjin, a term of abuse for someone who could not see reason, and it became an insult for people. The form tōhenboku-me appears in the sharebon 卯地臭意 (1783).
en.example: No matter how many times I explain, this blockhead asks the same thing again.

meaning: 人にへつらって機嫌を取る者。もとは宴席で客の遊びを盛り上げる男芸者、幇間のこと。
origin: 職業としての太鼓持ちは、豪遊が流行した元禄期に現れたと考えられている（宝暦ごろとする事典もある）。名の由来ははっきりせず、鳴り物の太鼓から来たとする説がある。豊臣秀吉の御伽衆・曽呂利新左衛門が「太閤、いかがで」と持ち上げたことから「太閤持ち」と呼ばれたという話も知られるが、曽呂利の実在も含めて伝承の域を出ない。
example: 課長の前では太鼓持ちになり、笑うところまで合わせている。

en.meaning: Someone who fawns on others to stay in their good graces. Originally a male entertainer (hōkan) who livened up guests' fun at banquets.
en.origin: Taikomochi as an occupation is thought to have appeared in the Genroku period, when lavish pleasure-seeking was in fashion (some encyclopedias place it around the Hōreki era). The source of the name is unclear; one theory derives it from the taiko drum used in musical accompaniment. There is also a well-known story that Sorori Shinzaemon, a member of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's otogishū (companions), was called taikō-mochi for flattering Hideyoshi with the words "Taikō, ikaga de" (How is it, my lord Taikō?). But this remains a legend, including whether Sorori existed at all.
en.example: In front of the section chief they turn into a flatterer, even laughing on cue.

meaning: 弱い者や不遇な者に同情して肩入れすること。「はんがんびいき」とも読む。
origin: 「判官」は九郎判官と呼ばれた源義経のこと。兄の頼朝に追われて非業の最期を遂げた義経に、人々が同情を寄せたことから生まれた。1638年の『毛吹草』に「世や花に判官贔屓春の風」の句がある。
example: 初出場の公立校をつい応援してしまうのは、判官贔屓というものだ。

en.meaning: Sympathizing with and taking the side of the weak or the unfortunate. Also read hangan-biiki.
en.origin: Hōgan refers to Minamoto no Yoshitsune, known as Kurō Hōgan. The phrase arose from the sympathy people felt for Yoshitsune, who was hunted down by his elder brother Yoritomo and met a tragic end. The Kefukigusa of 1638 contains the verse "Yo ya hana ni hōgan-biiki haru no kaze."
en.example: Finding yourself cheering for the public school making its first appearance is just rooting for the underdog.

meaning: わざと人の言うことに逆らう、ひねくれ者。もとは昔話に出てくる、人の心を探って邪魔をする悪い鬼のこと。
origin: 由来には諸説ある。記紀神話で邪心を持つ女神とされる天探女（あまのさぐめ）から来たという説があるが、民間語源説とみる辞書もある。仏教では毘沙門天の鎧の腹にある鬼面を海若（あまのじゃく）と呼び、のちに足下に踏まれた小鬼もそう呼ぶようになったとされる。昔話『瓜子姫』では姫に化ける悪役として登場する。
example: やめろと言われるとやりたくなる天邪鬼な性分だ。

en.meaning: A contrary person who deliberately goes against what others say. Originally a wicked demon in folktales that reads people's minds and gets in their way.
en.origin: There are several theories about its origin. One traces it to Ama no Sagume (天探女), a goddess with a wicked heart in the myths of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, though some dictionaries regard this as a folk etymology. In Buddhism, the demon face on the belly of Bishamonten's armor was called amanojaku (海若), and the name is said to have later been applied to the small demon trampled under his feet as well. In the folktale Urikohime it appears as the villain who disguises itself as the princess.
en.example: I'm a contrarian by nature: tell me not to do something and I want to do it.

meaning: 人情の機微に疎く、気がきかないこと。言動や趣味があか抜けないことも言う。
origin: 語源は未詳で、「野暮」は当て字。「野夫（やぶ）」が変化したとする説や、藪医者の「藪」とする説がある。江戸時代には「粋」「通」が理想とされ、その反対が野暮だった。ただし野暮は修行しだいで通になれるともされた。
example: いい雰囲気のところで終電の時間を聞くのは野暮というものだ。

en.meaning: Insensitive to the finer points of human feeling, and lacking tact. Also said of words, actions, or taste that lack polish.
en.origin: The origin is unknown, and 野暮 is ateji. One theory says it changed from yabu (野夫), another links it to the yabu of yabu-isha (quack doctor). In the Edo period iki (粋) and tsū (通) were held up as ideals, and yabo was their opposite. It was also held, however, that a yabo person could become tsū through practice.
en.example: Asking when the last train leaves just as the mood is getting good is tactless.

meaning: 自分で自分のことを褒めること。自慢。
origin: かつて味噌は家ごとに作っていたため味がそれぞれ違い、誰もが自分の家の味噌がいちばんうまいと思いがちだった。その自家製の味噌を自慢することから出た。1832年の滑稽本『大山道中膝栗毛』に用例がある。
example: 手前味噌になるが、今回の資料はよくできたと思う。

en.meaning: Praising oneself; bragging.
en.origin: Miso was once made in each household, so the flavor differed from home to home, and everyone tended to think their own family's miso was the best. The phrase comes from boasting about that homemade miso. An example appears in the comic book (kokkeibon) Ōyama Dōchū Hizakurige of 1832.
en.example: I don't mean to blow my own horn, but I think the handouts came out well this time.

meaning: 日が暮れて薄暗くなる夕方。たそがれ時。魔物に出会いやすい時刻とされた。
origin: もとは「大禍時（おおまがとき）」で、大きな災いが起こりがちな時刻の意。のちに「ま」が「魔」と意識され、「魔に逢う」の意も加わって「逢魔時」と書かれるようになった。漢の王莽にこじつけた「王莽時」という表記もある。
example: 子どものころ、逢魔が時までには家に帰れと祖母によく言われた。

en.gloss: dusk, the hour of meeting demons
en.meaning: The dim part of the evening after the sun has set; twilight. It was thought to be the hour when one was most likely to meet evil spirits.
en.origin: It was originally ōmagatoki (大禍時), meaning the hour when great misfortune tends to happen. Later the "ma" came to be understood as 魔 (demon), the sense of "meeting demons" was added, and the word came to be written 逢魔時. There is also a spelling, 王莽時, that ties it, through a far-fetched association, to Wang Mang of the Han.
en.example: When I was a child, my grandmother often told me to be home before ōmagatoki.

meaning: 干支の43番目で、60年に一度めぐってくる年。この年は火事が多く、生まれた女性は気性が激しく夫を食い殺すという根拠のない迷信がある。
origin: 五行説では丙も午も火にあたるため、火災の多い年とされた。この考えは中国から伝わり、江戸時代に都市住民の間に定着した。江戸前期の八百屋お七の放火事件と結びつけて語られることもある。1906年と1966年には迷信の影響で出生数が急減した。
example: 前回の丙午にあたる1966年は、迷信の影響で出生数が大きく減った。

en.meaning: The 43rd year of the sexagenary cycle, which comes around once every 60 years. There is a groundless superstition that fires are frequent in this year and that women born in it are fierce-tempered and will devour their husbands.
en.origin: In five-phase theory, both hinoe (丙) and uma (午) correspond to fire, so the year was considered one of many fires. The idea came from China and took hold among city dwellers in the Edo period. It is sometimes linked to the arson case of Yaoya Oshichi in the early Edo period. In 1906 and 1966, the number of births dropped sharply because of the superstition.
en.example: In 1966, the previous hinoeuma year, the number of births fell sharply because of the superstition.

meaning: 物事のよしあしを縁起で判断し、よい前兆を選んで悪い前兆を避けようとすること。
origin: 「縁起を担ぐ」から転じた言葉とみられる。「験（げん）」は「縁起」を逆さにした「ぎえん」が縮まったものとする説があるが、辞書では一説の扱い。「験」はもともと修行や加持祈祷のききめを指し、のちに吉凶の兆しの意でも使われるようになった。
example: 大事な商談の日は、験担ぎに同じネクタイを締めていく。

en.meaning: Judging things as good or bad by omens, choosing good signs and avoiding bad ones.
en.origin: It is thought to come from engi wo katsugu (縁起を担ぐ, to be superstitious about omens). One theory holds that gen (験) is a contraction of gien, a reversal of engi, but dictionaries treat this as only one theory. Gen originally meant the efficacy of ascetic practice or incantatory prayer, and later also came to be used for signs of good or bad fortune.
en.example: On the day of an important business meeting, I wear the same tie for luck.

meaning: 言葉に宿ると信じられた不思議な力。口にしたことがそのとおりに実現するとされた。
origin: 古代日本の信仰で、『万葉集』には日本を「言霊の幸はふ国」、つまり言葉の霊力が幸いをもたらす国と詠んだ歌がある。この信仰から、祝詞のように言葉の力を積極的に使う習わしと、縁起の悪い言葉を避ける忌み詞の風習が生まれた。
example: 言霊を気にして、受験生の前では「落ちる」という言葉を使わない。

en.gloss: the spirit that dwells in words
en.meaning: A mysterious power believed to reside in words. What was said aloud was thought to come true exactly as spoken.
en.origin: A belief of ancient Japan. The Man'yōshū contains a poem calling Japan "the land where kotodama bring blessings," that is, a country where the spiritual power of words brings good fortune. From this belief came both the practice of actively using the power of words, as in norito (Shinto prayers), and the custom of imikotoba, avoiding ill-omened words.
en.example: Mindful of kotodama, we avoid the word "fall" around students taking entrance exams.

meaning: 面倒で気が進まないこと。手間がかかりそうで腰が重い気持ちを表す。
origin: 「劫」はサンスクリット語 kalpa の音写で、きわめて長い時間の単位。億劫はその一億倍で、もとは「おっこう」「おくこう」と読み、途方もなく長い時間を指す仏教語だった。やり遂げるのに長い時間がかかることから「たやすくできない」、さらに「面倒で気が進まない」の意味に移り、読みも「おっくう」に変わった。
example: 雨の日は外に出るのが億劫だ。

sources.label: くらしの仏教語豆事典

en.meaning: Finding something a hassle and not feeling like doing it. It describes reluctance to get moving on something that looks like it will take effort.
en.origin: Kō (劫) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit kalpa, a unit of extremely long time. 億劫 is a hundred million times that. It was originally read okkō or okukō and was a Buddhist term for an unimaginably long period. Since something that takes a long time to accomplish cannot be done easily, the meaning shifted to "not easily done" and then to "bothersome, not inclined to do," and the reading also changed to okkū.
en.example: On rainy days, going outside feels like too much trouble.

meaning: つらさや欲求をこらえること。今はほめる意味で使われることが多い。
origin: 仏教では七種の慢心「七慢」の一つで、自我があると思い込んで自分を高く見て他人を見下す心を指す悪い意味の語だった。のちに自分に固執することから「我を張る・強情」の意味が生まれ、その意地の強さが「耐え忍ぶ」という良い意味に転じた。
example: 言い返したいのを我慢して、会議が終わるまで黙っていた。

en.meaning: Holding back pain or desires. Today it is mostly used approvingly.
en.origin: In Buddhism it was one of the seven kinds of pride (shichiman) and had a negative meaning: the mind that, convinced it has a self, rates itself highly and looks down on others. Later, from the idea of clinging to oneself, it came to mean being self-willed or stubborn, and that strength of will turned into the positive sense of enduring patiently.
en.example: I resisted the urge to answer back and kept quiet until the meeting ended.

meaning: 人と会ったときや別れるときに交わす言葉や礼。式でのスピーチの意味でも使う。
origin: 「挨」も「拶」も押す・迫るという意味の字。禅宗では「一挨一拶」といい、僧どうしが問答を重ねて相手の悟りの深さを試すことを指した。中世の禅僧が使っていたこの語がしだいに一般化し、ふだんの受け答えや礼儀の言葉を指すようになった。
example: 異動の初日に、部署の全員へ挨拶して回った。

en.meaning: Words or bows exchanged when meeting or parting. Also used for a speech at a ceremony.
en.origin: Both 挨 and 拶 are characters meaning to push or press. In Zen this was called ichiai issatsu (一挨一拶), referring to monks exchanging questions and answers to test the depth of each other's enlightenment. The word, used by Zen monks in the medieval period, gradually spread into general use and came to mean everyday exchanges and words of courtesy.
en.example: On my first day after the transfer, I went around greeting everyone in the department.

meaning: 遠回しに意地悪く相手を責めること。「皮肉な結果」のように、期待と逆になることも指す。
origin: もとは文字どおり「皮と肉」で、そこから「うわべ」の意味でも使われた。語源由来辞典などは、禅宗の祖・達磨の言葉とされる「皮肉骨髄」に由来すると説明する。骨髄が本質をつかんだ理解を表すのに対し、皮肉は表面だけの理解を表し、そこから相手をあてこする意味になったという説である。国語辞典は道元の清規にある「仏祖之皮肉骨髄」を古い用例に挙げるが、語源には触れていない。
example: 遅れて着いた私に、彼は「ずいぶんお早いご到着で」と皮肉を言った。

en.meaning: Criticizing someone indirectly and spitefully. It also refers to an outcome that is the opposite of what was expected, as in hiniku na kekka (an ironic result).
en.origin: It originally meant literally "skin and flesh," and from there was also used to mean "the surface." Sources such as Gogen Yurai Jiten explain that it comes from hiniku kotsuzui (skin, flesh, bone and marrow), words attributed to Bodhidharma (Daruma), the founder of Zen. In this theory, bone and marrow stand for an understanding that grasps the essence, while skin and flesh stand for a surface-level understanding, and from this the word came to mean making digs at someone. Japanese dictionaries cite busso no hiniku kotsuzui (仏祖之皮肉骨髄) from Dōgen's monastic rules (shingi) as an early example but do not address the etymology.
en.example: When I arrived late, he said sarcastically, "What an early arrival."

meaning: 後ろに打ち消しをつけて「絶対に〜ない」と強く言い切る語。
origin: 仏教の宇宙観では、大地は風輪・水輪・金輪の三層の上に乗っているとされる。そのうち金輪と水輪の境目が金輪際で、大地のいちばん底にあたる。そこから「とことん」「どこまでも」の意味が生まれた。江戸時代には打ち消しなしでも使われたが、今は「金輪際〜しない」の形がほとんどだ。
example: あの店には金輪際行かない。

en.meaning: A word followed by a negative to declare strongly that something will absolutely never happen.
en.origin: In Buddhist cosmology, the earth is said to rest on three layers: the wind wheel, the water wheel and the metal wheel (konrin). The boundary between the metal wheel and the water wheel is konrinzai, the very bottom of the earth. From this came the senses "thoroughly" and "to the very end." In the Edo period it was also used without a negative, but today it almost always appears in the form konrinzai ... shinai (will never ...).
en.example: I am never going to that restaurant again.

meaning: うれしさのあまり舞い上がり、周りが見えなくなっている状態。
origin: 仏教で、迷いの世界である三界（有）のいちばん上にある天を指す。どの天かは、無色界の最上の非想非非想天とする説と、色界の最上の色究竟天とする説がある。その頂にのぼりつめる意から、得意の絶頂や、夢中で我を忘れる様子を言うようになった。
example: 企画が初めて通って有頂天になっていた。

en.meaning: So elated that one gets carried away and loses sight of everything around.
en.origin: In Buddhism it refers to the highest heaven of the three realms of existence (u), the world of delusion. Views differ on which heaven this is: one theory says Hisō-hihisō-ten (非想非非想天), the top of the formless realm, and another says Shikikukyō-ten (色究竟天), the top of the form realm. From the idea of climbing all the way to that summit, it came to describe the height of triumph or being so absorbed that one forgets oneself.
en.example: My proposal had been approved for the first time, and I was on cloud nine.

meaning: 意気込んで向かったのにかわされたり、期待外れで拍子抜けしたりすること。「肩透かしを食う」の形でよく使う。
origin: 相撲の決まり手の一つ。相手の腕のつけ根に手を浅く引っかけて引きながら体を開き、もう一方の手で肩をはたいて前に落とす。突進してくる勢いをまともに受けずにかわす技なので、相手の勢いをそらすことのたとえになった。
example: 大発表があると身構えていたら、ただの席替えで肩透かしを食った。

en.meaning: Charging in eagerly only to be sidestepped, or being let down when something falls short of expectations. Often used in the form katasukashi wo kuu (to be let down).
en.origin: One of the winning techniques (kimarite) in sumo. The wrestler lightly hooks a hand under the base of the opponent's arm, pulls while turning the body aside, and slaps the opponent's shoulder with the other hand to send them falling forward. Because it dodges a charging opponent's momentum instead of meeting it head on, it became a figure for deflecting someone's momentum.
en.example: We braced ourselves for a big announcement, but it was only a seating change, which was quite a letdown.

meaning: 調子に乗って先走り、やりすぎたり失敗したりすること。
origin: 相撲で、相手を土俵際まで追い詰めながら、勢い余って自分の足を先に土俵の外へ出して負けること。決まり手とは区別される、自分の動作による負けの一つ。勝ちが目の前なのに勢いで自滅する形が、そのまま比喩になった。
example: 決まる前に取引先へ話してしまったのは勇み足だった。

en.meaning: Getting carried away and rushing ahead, overdoing things or making a mistake.
en.origin: In sumo, losing by stepping out of the ring first through excess momentum while driving the opponent to the edge. It is one of the losses caused by a wrestler's own action, distinguished from the kimarite (winning techniques). The picture of beating oneself through sheer momentum with victory in sight became the figure of speech as is.
en.example: Telling the client before the deal was final was jumping the gun.

meaning: うまくいかなかった話し合いや勝負を、いったん止めて最初からやり直すこと。
origin: 相撲で、立ち合いの呼吸が合わず、仕切りをもう一度やり直すこと。そこから試合や勝負のやり直し、さらに交渉を初めからやり直す意味でも使われるようになった。
example: 議論が行き詰まったので、来週に仕切り直すことにした。

en.meaning: Halting a talk or contest that is not going well and starting again from the beginning.
en.origin: In sumo, redoing the shikiri (the crouching ritual before the charge) when the two wrestlers' timing at the initial charge does not match. From there it came to mean restarting a match or contest, and also starting negotiations over from the beginning.
en.example: The discussion had reached a dead end, so we decided to start over next week.

meaning: その人がいちばん得意な芸や持ちネタ。よく出る口癖や決まった動作を指すこともある。
origin: 七代目市川團十郎が天保3年（1832）、市川家の得意演目を「歌舞伎十八番」として示し、これが得意芸を指す語として広まった。「おはこ」は大切な物を箱にしまう「箱入り」の略とされ、十八番の台本を箱に入れて保存したからという説もある。ただし、歌舞伎役者の秘蔵の当たり芸を以前から「十八番」と呼んでいたことによる当て字とみる辞典もあり、定説はない。
example: 部長はカラオケで必ず十八番の演歌を歌う。

en.meaning: The art or routine a person does best. It can also refer to a habitual phrase or a characteristic gesture.
en.origin: In Tenpō 3 (1832), Ichikawa Danjūrō VII presented the Ichikawa family's signature plays as the Kabuki Jūhachiban (Eighteen Kabuki Plays), and the term spread as a word for one's specialty. Ohako is said to be short for hakoiri (kept in a box), meaning something precious put away in a box, and one theory holds that this is because the scripts of the eighteen plays were stored in boxes. However, some dictionaries regard the spelling as ateji based on the earlier practice of calling a kabuki actor's treasured hit pieces jūhachiban, and there is no settled view.
en.example: At karaoke, our department head always sings their signature enka song.

meaning: 前の人と同じ失敗を繰り返すこと。「二の舞を演じる」「二の舞を踏む」の形で使う。
origin: 雅楽の舞楽「二ノ舞」が由来。「安摩」のすぐ後に、笑った面の老爺と腫れた面の老婆が出てきて、安摩をまねて滑稽に舞う。この、まねをしてうまくいかない舞から、人のまねをして同じ失敗をする意味になった。
example: 前のプロジェクトの二の舞にならないよう、日程に余裕を持たせた。

en.meaning: Making the same mistake as someone before. Used in the forms ninomai wo enjiru and ninomai wo fumu.
en.origin: It comes from Ni no Mai, a bugaku court dance. Right after the dance Ama, an old man in a laughing mask and an old woman in a swollen-faced mask appear and dance comically in imitation of Ama. From this dance, an imitation that does not quite work, the word came to mean copying others and making the same mistake.
en.example: We built slack into the schedule so as not to repeat what happened on the last project.

meaning: 表に出ず、裏で人や物事を操っている人物。
origin: もとは歌舞伎で使う黒い幕。場面転換で舞台を隠したり、夜や闇を表す背景にしたりする。死んだ役を小さな黒い幕で隠して引っ込ませる使い方もある。歌舞伎では黒は見えないものの約束なので、そこから陰で糸を引く人を指すようになった。
example: 今回の人事には、裏で糸を引く黒幕がいるらしい。

en.meaning: A person who stays out of sight and manipulates people or events from behind the scenes.
en.origin: Originally the black curtain used in kabuki. It hides the stage during scene changes or serves as a backdrop representing night or darkness. A small black curtain is also used to screen a character who has died so the actor can leave the stage. Since in kabuki black by convention stands for what cannot be seen, the word came to mean someone pulling strings in the shadows.
en.example: Word is that someone is pulling the strings behind this round of personnel changes.

meaning: 一般の観客や世間の人々。「大向こうを唸らせる」は、見事な腕前で多くの人を感心させること。
origin: 劇場で舞台から見て正面後方にある立見の場所、一幕見の席を指した。そこには芝居通の客が多く、その観客を感心させるのは本物の芸だけというところから、今の言い方が生まれた。「向こうを唸らせる」は誤り。
example: 彼女の発表は大向こうを唸らせる出来だった。

sources.label: コトバンク（大向こうを唸らせる）

en.meaning: Ordinary audiences, or people at large. Ōmukō wo unaraseru means to impress a great many people with outstanding skill.
en.origin: It referred to the standing area at the back of the theater, directly opposite the stage, where the hitomakumi (single-act) seats were. Many seasoned theatergoers gathered there, and only genuine artistry could impress them, which gave rise to the present expression. Mukō wo unaraseru (without ō) is incorrect.
en.example: Her presentation was good enough to win over the whole crowd.

meaning: 勝敗や運命を決める大事な分かれ目。スポーツの大一番によく使う。
origin: 天王山は京都府大山崎町にある山。天正10年（1582）、そのふもとの山崎の戦いで羽柴秀吉が明智光秀を破った。この山を押さえたことが勝敗を決めたと伝えられ、勝負の分かれ目のたとえになった。ただし、実際には山の占拠はそれほど大きな意味を持たなかったとする見方もある。
example: この三連戦が優勝争いの天王山になる。

en.meaning: The crucial turning point that decides victory or defeat, or one's fate. Often used of a big match in sports.
en.origin: Tennōzan is a mountain in Ōyamazaki, Kyoto Prefecture. In Tenshō 10 (1582), at the Battle of Yamazaki at its foot, Hashiba Hideyoshi defeated Akechi Mitsuhide. Taking this mountain is said to have decided the outcome, so it became a figure for the turning point of a contest. There is also a view, however, that occupying the mountain did not actually matter much.
en.example: This three-game series will be the decisive stretch of the pennant race.

reading: おだわらひょうじょう
meaning: いつまでも話し合うばかりで、なかなか結論が出ない会議。
origin: 天正18年（1590）、豊臣秀吉に小田原城を囲まれた北条氏は、籠城か出撃か、戦うか和睦かで評定を重ねたが、方針が決まらず日を過ごした。結局は降伏し、戦国大名としての北条氏は滅んだ。北条氏が下級武士も加えた合議の仕組みを持っていたため議論が長引いた、とする説もある。
example: 会議が小田原評定にならないよう、最後に誰が決めるかを先に決めておく。

en.meaning: A meeting where people keep talking and never reach a conclusion.
en.origin: In Tenshō 18 (1590), with Odawara Castle besieged by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the Hōjō clan held council (hyōjō) after council on whether to hold the castle or sally out, and whether to fight or make peace, but could not settle on a course and let the days go by. In the end they surrendered, and the Hōjō as a Sengoku daimyō house came to an end. One theory holds that the debate dragged on because the Hōjō had a council system that included lower-ranking samurai.
en.example: So the meeting doesn't turn into endless debate, we decide in advance who makes the final call.

meaning: 権力や地位を手に入れても、ごく短い間で失うこと。
origin: 天正10年（1582）、明智光秀は本能寺で織田信長を討って天下を取ったが、山崎の戦いで羽柴秀吉に敗れた。その期間の短さを「三日」と言い表したもの。辞書によれば、実際の期間は13日ほどだった。
example: 首位に立ったのもつかの間、翌週には抜かれて三日天下に終わった。

en.meaning: Gaining power or a position only to lose it after a very short time.
en.origin: In Tenshō 10 (1582), Akechi Mitsuhide killed Oda Nobunaga at Honnōji and seized power, but was defeated by Hashiba Hideyoshi at the Battle of Yamazaki. The shortness of that period is expressed as "three days." According to dictionaries, the actual period was about 13 days.
en.example: We had barely taken first place when we were overtaken the following week, so our reign at the top was short-lived.

meaning: 人の話や振る舞いに、横からやじや冷やかしの言葉をかけること。
origin: 「半畳」は江戸期の芝居小屋で、土間の客が尻に敷いた一人用の小さな敷物。役者の芸が気に入らないと、客がこれを舞台へ投げ込んで不満を示した。そこから、他人の言動を非難したりからかったりする意味になった。「半畳を打ち込む」「半畳を言う」ともいう。
example: 発表の最中に、後ろから半畳を入れる人がいた。

en.meaning: To call out jeers or mocking remarks from the side at what someone is saying or doing.
en.origin: A hanjō (half mat) was a small one-person mat that spectators in the pit (doma) of Edo-period playhouses sat on. When they did not like an actor's performance, they threw it onto the stage to show their displeasure. From this it came to mean criticizing or making fun of what others say or do. Also hanjō wo uchikomu or hanjō wo iu.
en.example: During the presentation, someone at the back kept heckling.

meaning: 自信のほどを見せつけるため、大げさな態度で言い切ること。できもしないことをできると言う場合にも使う。
origin: 歌舞伎の「見得」から。感情が頂点に達した場面で、役者が一瞬動きを止め、にらむようにして決めるポーズのことだ。とりわけ際立った見得を切ることを「大見得を切る」といい、一般の言葉に広がった。
example: 来月までに全部終わらせると大見得を切ってしまった。

en.meaning: To declare something with an exaggerated show of confidence. Also used when someone claims they can do what they cannot.
en.origin: From the kabuki mie, the pose an actor strikes at an emotional climax, freezing for a moment with a glaring stare. Striking an especially bold mie is called ōmie wo kiru, and the phrase spread into everyday language.
en.example: I went and boldly declared that I would finish everything by next month.

meaning: 経験を積んで、仕事ぶりや態度がその立場にしっくりなじむこと。服装や身のこなしが似合ってきたときにもいう。
origin: 「板」は芝居の舞台のこと。役者が場数を踏み、芸が舞台によく調和するようになった状態をいった。それが役者以外にも広く使われるようになった。
example: 最初はぎこちなかった彼女の店長ぶりも、すっかり板に付いてきた。

en.meaning: With experience, one's work and manner come to fit one's position naturally. Also said when clothes or bearing start to suit someone.
en.origin: Ita (boards) means the theater stage. It described an actor who, after many performances, had come to fit naturally on the stage. It then came to be used widely for people other than actors.
en.example: She was awkward as store manager at first, but she has really grown into the role.

meaning: 一度よくなったものが、またつまらない元の状態に戻ってしまうこと。それまでの苦労が無駄になったときに使う。
origin: 語源ははっきりしない。よく知られるのは『天正記』にあるとされる話で、戦国大名の筒井順昭が死んだとき、子の順慶が幼かったため死を伏せ、声の似た木阿弥という男を寝所に寝かせて身代わりにした。順慶が成長すると木阿弥は元の町人に戻ったという。ほかに、修行を怠って元の妻のもとへ戻った僧の話や、朱塗りがはげて木地が出た「元の木椀」から来たとする説もあり、用例は室町末から江戸初めの狂言台本に見える。
example: 三キロ痩せたのに、年末の飲み会続きで元の木阿弥になった。

en.meaning: Something that had once improved slips back into its old, unremarkable state. Used when earlier effort has gone to waste.
en.origin: The origin is unclear. The best-known story is said to appear in the Tenshōki: when the warlord Tsutsui Junshō died, his son Junkei was still young, so the death was kept secret and a man named Mokuami, whose voice resembled Junshō's, was laid in his bedchamber as a stand-in. When Junkei grew up, Mokuami went back to being an ordinary townsman. Other theories trace it to a monk who neglected his training and went back to his former wife, or to moto no mokuwan, a lacquered bowl whose vermilion has worn off to reveal the bare wood. Examples appear in kyōgen scripts from the late Muromachi to the early Edo period.
en.example: I lost three kilos, but a run of year-end drinking parties put me right back where I started.

word: 売り家と唐様で書く三代目
reading: うりいえとからようでかくさんだいめ
meaning: 初代が苦労して築いた家も、三代目になると遊びにふけって潰してしまうという皮肉。商売はだめでも趣味だけは一流、という跡取りをからかうときに使う。
origin: もとは川柳。没落した三代目が家を売りに出すが、その「売り家」の札の字は、江戸時代の学者の間で流行った中国風の書体「唐様」でしゃれている。商売そっちのけで遊芸におぼれていた暮らしが、筆跡からうかがえるという笑いである。
example: ワインの蘊蓄ばかりで経営に身の入らない三代目を見ると、売り家と唐様で書く三代目という川柳を思い出す。

en.gloss: the third generation sells the house
en.meaning: A wry saying that a house the founder built through hard work is ruined by the third generation, who lives for pleasure. Used to mock an heir who is hopeless at business but first-rate at hobbies.
en.origin: Originally a senryū. The ruined third-generation heir puts the house up for sale, but the characters on the "house for sale" sign are written stylishly in karayō, a Chinese-style calligraphy fashionable among Edo-period scholars. The joke is that the handwriting reveals a life spent absorbed in the leisure arts while the business was neglected.
en.example: Seeing a third-generation owner who can talk about wine endlessly but puts no effort into running the company, I think of the senryū about the heir who writes "house for sale" in elegant Chinese script.

word: 江戸の敵を長崎で討つ
reading: えどのかたきをながさきでうつ
meaning: 意外な場所で、あるいは筋違いのことで、以前の恨みを晴らすこと。
origin: 楳垣実の説では、もとの形は「江戸の敵を長崎が討つ」。文政のころ、大坂の見世物師が江戸で大当たりして江戸の見世物を圧倒したが、まもなく長崎の職人の見世物がそれを上回る人気を取り、長崎が江戸の仇を討った格好になったという。籠細工をめぐる職人同士の面目争いとして紹介する辞典もある。ただし一説にすぎず、語源は確定していない。
example: 会議で反対された恨みを歓迎会の店選びで晴らすのは、江戸の敵を長崎で討つようなものだ。

en.gloss: getting even in an unexpected place
en.meaning: Settling an old grudge in an unexpected place, or over an unrelated matter.
en.origin: According to Umegaki Minoru, the original form was Edo no kataki wo Nagasaki ga utsu (Nagasaki avenges Edo). In the Bunsei era, a showman from Osaka had a great hit in Edo and overwhelmed the Edo shows, but soon a show by Nagasaki craftsmen surpassed it in popularity, so it was as if Nagasaki had avenged Edo. Some dictionaries present it as a contest of pride between craftsmen over basketwork figures (kagozaiku). This is only one theory, however, and the origin has not been established.
en.example: Getting back at people who opposed you in a meeting through your choice of restaurant for the welcome party is like avenging Edo in Nagasaki.

meaning: 自分に都合がいいように、数を実際より多く、あるいは少なくごまかして言うこと。年齢についてよく使う。
origin: 語源には諸説ある。魚市場で小魚を早口で数える「いさば読み（魚市読み）」が縮まったという説、大量の鯖を数えるときに使用人がごまかしたからという説、傷みやすい鯖は急いで売るので数え方が雑だったからという説、刺鯖を二枚重ねで一連と数えたことから来たという説などだ。用例は1753年の談義本にすでに見える。
example: プロフィールの年齢を三つ鯖を読んでいた。

en.meaning: To give a number as higher or lower than it really is, to suit oneself. Often used about age.
en.origin: There are several theories. One says it is a contraction of isaba-yomi (魚市読み), the rapid counting of small fish at fish markets. Others say it comes from workers cheating when counting large numbers of mackerel, from mackerel spoiling quickly and being sold in a hurry so the counting was sloppy, or from the practice of counting two sashisaba (salted split mackerel) laid one on top of the other as a single unit. An example already appears in a dangibon (comic sermon book) from 1753.
en.example: They had fudged the age on their profile by three years.

meaning: 物事がいつまでも片づかず、話が前に進まないこと。
origin: 「埒」はもともと馬場の周りに巡らした柵のこと。上賀茂神社の神事として行われる競馬（くらべうま）から出た語だとする辞典もある。「物事の区切り」という比喩の使い方は中世後期ごろからとみられ、『日葡辞書』に「埒が明く」の用例がある。今は主に打ち消しの形で使う。
example: メールでは埒が明かないので、直接電話して確かめた。

en.meaning: A matter drags on without being settled, and the discussion makes no progress.
en.origin: Rachi (埒) originally meant the fence around a riding ground. Some dictionaries say the expression comes from kurabeuma, the horse races held as a Shinto ritual at Kamigamo Shrine. The figurative use meaning "a settled point" or "a conclusion" is thought to date from around the late medieval period, and the Nippo Jisho has an example of rachi ga aku. Today it is mainly used in the negative.
en.example: Email was getting us nowhere, so I called them directly to confirm.

reading: よめとおめかさのうち
meaning: 夜の暗がりや遠くから見たとき、笠で顔が一部隠れているときは、細部が見えないぶん実際より美しく見えるということ。主に女性についていう。
origin: 「夜目遠目」だけなら、ものがぼんやり見えるというだけの意味。「笠の内」が付くことで人、特に女性の容姿の話になる。「笠」は雨傘や日傘とする見方もある。江戸初期の俳諧集『犬子集』（1633）に用例がある。
example: 夜目遠目笠の内というとおり、写真の印象と実物はかなり違った。

en.gloss: looking better by night, from afar, or under a hat
en.meaning: Seen at night, from far away, or with the face partly hidden under a hat, a person looks more beautiful than they really are because the details cannot be made out. Said mainly of women.
en.origin: Yome tōme (seen at night, seen from afar) on its own means only that things look blurry. Adding kasa no uchi (under a hat) makes it about people, especially women's looks. Some take kasa to mean an umbrella or parasol. An example appears in the early Edo haikai collection Enokoshū (1633).
en.example: As the saying about night, distance, and hats goes, the person in real life was quite different from the impression the photos gave.

word: 武士は食わねど高楊枝
reading: ぶしはくわねどたかようじ
meaning: 貧しくても気位を高く保ち、みっともない振る舞いはしないこと。今は、苦しいのに平気なふりをするやせ我慢を、からかって言うことも多い。
origin: 武士は食事にありつけなくても、満腹したような顔でゆうゆうと楊枝を使ってみせる、という姿から。古くは「侍は」の形で、江戸中期以降に「武士は」が主流になった。下級武士の苦しい暮らしを踏まえれば、町人から武士への皮肉とも読める。
example: 給料日前で金がないのに後輩の分まで払うのは、武士は食わねど高楊枝だ。

en.gloss: a samurai picks his teeth unfed
en.meaning: Keeping one's pride and not behaving shamefully even when poor. Today it is also often used teasingly for putting on a brave face while struggling.
en.origin: From the image of a samurai who, even with nothing to eat, leisurely uses a toothpick as if he had eaten his fill. The older form began with samurai wa, and bushi wa became the main form from the mid-Edo period on. Given the hard lives of lower-ranking samurai, it can also be read as townspeople's sarcasm aimed at samurai.
en.example: Paying for your juniors as well when you are broke before payday is pure samurai pride.

reading: おにもじゅうはちばんちゃもでばな
meaning: 器量がよくない人でも、年ごろになればそれなりの魅力が出てくるということ。
origin: 鬼でも年ごろになれば少しは美しく見え、粗末な番茶でも淹れたては香りがいい、という二つのたとえを並べたもの。今は女性に使うが、古くは男女どちらにも使った。類句に「鬼も十七茨も花」「鬼も十七山茶も煮端」がある。前半の「鬼も十八」は江戸初期の咄本『醒睡笑』に用例がある。
example: 鬼も十八番茶も出花で、親戚の娘も年ごろになってずいぶん垢抜けた。

en.gloss: even a demon is pretty at eighteen
en.meaning: Even someone not especially good-looking gains a certain charm on reaching young adulthood.
en.origin: It pairs two images: even a demon looks somewhat attractive at the right age, and even coarse bancha tea smells good when freshly brewed. Today it is used of women, but in the past it was used of both men and women. Similar sayings include oni mo jūshichi ibara mo hana (a demon at seventeen, a thorn bush in flower) and 鬼も十七山茶も煮端 (a demon at seventeen, coarse mountain tea freshly brewed). The first half, oni mo jūhachi, appears in the early Edo collection of humorous tales Seisuishō.
en.example: Even a demon is pretty at eighteen, as they say, and my relative's daughter has become quite polished now that she is grown.

meaning: 悪事を続けてきた者が、とうとう捕まって罪に服するとき。転じて、物事に見切りをつけて覚悟を決めるとき。
origin: 滞納していた年貢を清算する時期、というのが元の意味。そこから、悪人が捕まって罪に服する場面を指すようになった。今では、気ままな独身生活に区切りをつけるときなどにも冗談まじりで使う。
example: 遊び歩いていた彼も、年貢の納め時と観念して婚約した。

en.meaning: The moment when someone who has long been doing wrong is finally caught and pays for it. By extension, the time to give something up and resign oneself to what must be done.
en.origin: The original meaning was the time to settle overdue nengu (annual land tax). From there it came to refer to a wrongdoer being caught and submitting to punishment. Today it is also used jokingly, for example when someone ends a carefree single life.
en.example: Even he, after years of running around, accepted that his time was up and got engaged.

reading: ひだりうちわでくらす
meaning: あくせく働かなくても安楽に暮らせること。
origin: 利き手でない左手で、ゆうゆうと団扇をあおぐ姿から。そこから、のんびり安楽に暮らす意味になった。扇を使う「左扇」も同じ意味。「左団扇」は1784年の洒落本に用例がある。
example: 家賃収入だけで左団扇で暮らせる身分がうらやましい。

en.meaning: To live comfortably without having to work hard.
en.origin: From the image of someone leisurely fanning themselves with a round fan (uchiwa) held in the left, non-dominant hand. From this it came to mean living a relaxed, easy life. Hidari ōgi, with a folding fan, means the same. Hidari uchiwa appears in a sharebon from 1784.
en.example: I envy people who can live in comfort on rental income alone.

meaning: もう後がない、最後の決断を迫られる場面。進退きわまった状況をいう。
origin: もとは近世に首切りの刑を行うために築いた土の壇、またはその刑場のこと。そこから、追い詰められて逃げ場のない最後の局面を指すようになった。刑場の意味では1772年の咄本に、比喩の意味では1908年の小説に用例がある。
example: 土壇場で予約を取り消すことになり、店に平謝りした。

en.gloss: the last minute, the eleventh hour
en.meaning: A point with no way back, where a final decision must be made. Describes a situation where one is completely cornered.
en.origin: Originally an earthen platform built in the early modern period for carrying out beheadings, or the execution ground itself. From this it came to mean the final stage where one is cornered with no escape. The execution-ground sense appears in a hanashibon (book of humorous tales) from 1772, and the figurative sense in a novel from 1908.
en.example: We had to cancel the reservation at the last minute and apologized profusely to the restaurant.
